Source: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations.

questions.prompt: Halden Freight's invoice bot follows a fixed script: when the total matches the purchase order it approves, otherwise it sends the invoice to a clerk. Nothing in it learns or reasons. Which of the five levels is this?

options.text: Agentic Workflows
Semi-Automatic Agents
Rule-Based Automation
Intelligent Automation

questions.explanation: A fixed if-then script with no learning is the lowest level, Rule-Based Automation. Intelligent Automation would add a learned or AI component to the automated flow. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI system plans each purchase order by itself but pauses and waits for a buyer to approve before it places any order. Which of the five levels fits best?

options.text: Semi-Automatic Agents
Full-Autonomous Agents
Rule-Based Automation
Intelligent Automation

questions.explanation: The system plans and acts like an agent, yet a person must approve its actions, which points to the fourth level. Full-Autonomous Agents would place the orders with no approval step. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps of a basic RAG request in order.

options.text: The model generates an answer from the augmented prompt
The passages are added to the prompt as grounding data
The application retrieves relevant passages from an index
The user asks a question

questions.explanation: RAG runs retrieve, then augment, then generate. Retrieval must come before generation, because the model can only ground its answer in passages that are already in its prompt. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of RAG in an LLM solution?

options.text: Grounding answers in retrieved data the model was not trained on
Retraining the weights of the model each night on new files
Encrypting documents before they are passed to the model
Compressing prompts so that each request uses far fewer input tokens

questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant content and places it in the prompt, so answers can draw on private or current data. It does not change the model's weights, which is what distinguishes it from retraining or fine-tuning. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: Odell Health's policy assistant must answer from documents that change every week and show which document each answer came from. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Fine-tuning once on last year's documents
A higher temperature for broader answers
RAG over an index of the current documents
A longer system prompt that demands accuracy

questions.explanation: RAG reads the current documents at question time and can cite them. Fine-tuning is the tempting alternative, but a fine-tuned model is frozen at its training data and cannot point to a source document. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: A RAG assistant gives a confident but wrong answer. The logs show that the retriever returned passages about a different product. What does this show?

options.text: Adding retrieval always removes the risk of a hallucination
The passages returned were too long to fit the context window
Grounding is only as good as the passages that retrieval returns
The model's training data has to be older than the search index

questions.explanation: If retrieval returns irrelevant passages, the model can still produce an inaccurate answer. The belief that retrieval removes hallucination is the trap: RAG reduces guessing, but it depends on retrieval quality. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: Which description matches composite AI?

options.text: Chaining several prompts to the same LLM in a single chat
Merging the training data of two vendors into one shared model
Combining machine learning, rules and LLMs in one solution
Running one very large model for all tasks in a company

questions.explanation: The study guide describes composite AI as combining machine learning, rules-based systems and LLMs. Chaining prompts to one LLM is a prompting technique and still uses a single kind of AI. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations.

questions.prompt: Quarry Insurance scores claims with a fraud model, applies fixed regulatory rules to each payout, and uses an LLM to draft the customer letter. What is this design an example of?

options.text: Composite AI
Prompt chaining
Multimodal AI
Fine-tuning

questions.explanation: Three different techniques, a learned model, fixed rules and an LLM, work together in one solution, which is composite AI. Multimodal AI is about one model handling several input types such as text and images. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations.

questions.prompt: Match each component of an AI agent to what it does.

options.text: Keeping the conversation history and state
Calling functions, APIs or systems to take action
Reasoning about the request and deciding the next step
Setting the scope, boundaries and expected behaviour
Shrinking the model so that replies arrive faster

questions.explanation: An agent uses a model to reason, instructions to bound it, tools to act and memory for continuity. Tools and memory are the pair most often confused: tools change or read the outside world, memory keeps state. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: What most clearly separates an AI agent from a plain LLM chat?

options.text: It decides on steps and calls tools to act toward a goal
It was trained on a much larger set of public web documents
It stores each answer so that none is repeated later
It answers faster because it skips the reasoning stage

questions.explanation: An agent uses a model to choose actions and tools over several steps, while a plain chat only returns text. Training-set size is the tempting answer, but an agent and a chat can run on exactly the same model. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: A team gives an LLM a goal, a calendar API and an email API. It checks availability, proposes a slot, sends invitations and tries again when someone declines. Which term describes the whole system?

options.text: A fine-tuned model
A prompt template
A vector index
An AI agent

questions.explanation: A model that pursues a goal by choosing and calling tools across several steps is an agent. A prompt template only shapes one request and cannot call the calendar or react to a decline. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: Why do agents call for more testing and governance than a standard RAG application?

options.text: The model chooses its own steps and tools, so runs can differ
Their answers are stored in memory and cannot be removed afterwards
They need a separate model for each tool they can call
Their retrieval is slower than in a fixed RAG pipeline

questions.explanation: Standard RAG follows a fixed retrieval flow, while an agent lets the model decide what to do at each step, which makes behaviour nondeterministic. Speed is not the issue; unpredictability of actions is. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: Match each AI term to its meaning.

options.text: The amount of text a model can consider at once
A saved copy of the weights of a model
A numeric representation used for similarity search
A fluent output that is false or unsupported
A chunk of text that a model reads or writes

questions.explanation: Tokens are the units of text, embeddings are numeric representations, the context window is the working limit and a hallucination is a confident falsehood. Token and context window are the usual mix-up: the window is measured in tokens. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What happens during inference?

options.text: A trained model produces an output for a new input
Raw data is cleaned and split into separate sets
Engineers compare model designs on a benchmark
The weights of a model are adjusted using examples

questions.explanation: Inference is using a trained model to produce an output. Adjusting weights from examples is training, the phase that comes before inference and the one it is most often confused with. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Verano Travel wants its assistant to write in the brand's voice consistently across thousands of replies, and examples in the prompt have not been enough. The facts it needs are already supplied. Which customisation targets this most directly?

options.text: A lower price per token
A larger context window
A vector index of fare rules
Fine-tuning on approved samples

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning adapts how a model behaves and writes, which suits a persistent style need. A vector index is the tempting answer, but retrieval supplies facts, and the facts are not what is missing here. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does raising the temperature setting of an LLM do to its output?

options.text: Makes it shorter and more factual
Makes it draw on a much longer prompt
Makes it reflect more recent data
Makes it more varied and less predictable

questions.explanation: Temperature controls randomness in token selection, so a higher value gives more varied output. It does not make answers more factual; if anything, a lower temperature is used when consistency matters. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An LLM cites a court case in a legal summary, and the case turns out to be invented. Which term names this failure?

options.text: Data drift
Hallucination
Prompt injection
Overfitting

questions.explanation: A fluent, confident statement that is false or unsupported is a hallucination. Prompt injection is an attack that changes the model's behaviour through crafted input, and nobody attacked the model here. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a copilot?

options.text: An assistant that works beside a user and suggests things to accept or edit
An agent that completes an entire process with no person involved at all
A script that replays recorded clicks in an existing line-of-business application
A model that a company trains from scratch using its own private data

questions.explanation: A copilot works alongside a person and offers suggestions the person can accept, reject or change. An agent that finishes the whole process alone is an autonomous agent, the contrast the same source draws. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agents in Azure Cosmos DB (copilots and autonomous agents).

questions.prompt: A marketing lead who cannot code wants a reusable assistant that follows the brand guide and can consult three uploaded reference files. What is the simplest fit?

options.text: A fine-tuned vision model on dedicated servers
A new foundation model trained for the department
A custom GPT with instructions and knowledge files
A data warehouse with nightly reporting files

questions.explanation: A custom GPT packages instructions and reference files into a reusable assistant without code. Training a new foundation model would be far more than the need requires, and the lead has neither the data nor the skills. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A custom GPT answers questions from uploaded files but cannot update the CRM. What would have to be added for it to do so?

options.text: More example chats in its knowledge files
An action that connects it to the CRM's API
A higher temperature for creative replies
A longer set of instructions about the CRM system

questions.explanation: To change another system an assistant needs a tool or action that calls that system. More instructions only change what it says; they give it no way to reach the CRM. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A task needs one summary of a document that a person supplies and then reviews. Which choice is proportionate?

options.text: An autonomous agent, since agents outperform plain prompts
A multi-agent system, since summaries benefit from debate
A fine-tuned model, since each document will be different
A single LLM prompt, since no tools or planning are needed

questions.explanation: A one-step task with the content supplied needs only a prompt. An agent adds autonomy and with it unpredictability and governance effort, which is justified by multi-step work with tools, not by a summary. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a model that accepts an image together with a text question and answers in text?

options.text: Multi-agent
Multimodal
Retrieval-augmented
Fine-tuned

questions.explanation: A multimodal model handles more than one type of input or output, such as images and text. Multi-agent sounds similar but describes several agents cooperating, whatever kinds of input they take. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why can the same prompt give an LLM different answers on different runs?

options.text: It searches the web again on each run and finds new pages
It retrains itself a little after every answer that it gives
It keeps a random seed for each user that changes daily
It samples each next token from a probability distribution

questions.explanation: An LLM writes by repeatedly choosing the next token from a probability distribution, so with sampling switched on, two runs can differ. A plain LLM neither browses the web nor retrains between answers; those abilities need extra tools or a new training run. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Fennick Media asks an LLM for last week's exchange rates and gets confident but out-of-date figures. What explains this best?

options.text: Its temperature setting was set too low
Language models cannot work with numbers at all
Its knowledge stops at its training cut-off
The prompt was too short for an accurate reply

questions.explanation: A model knows only what was in its training data, which ends at a cut-off date, so recent facts must be supplied in the prompt or retrieved at question time. A low temperature makes output more predictable; it does not make the model's knowledge any more current. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a foundation model?

options.text: A rules engine that sits underneath every machine learning system
A small model built from scratch for one narrow business task
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks
The first internal version of a model, before it is released to customers

questions.explanation: Foundation models are trained once on broad data and then adapted, by prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning, to many tasks; LLMs are the best-known example. A narrow model built for one task is the opposite idea. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A product team must sort 40,000 support emails into five fixed categories each night. Which statement about using generative AI here is most accurate?

options.text: A trained classifier could do it more cheaply and consistently
Language tasks need generative AI because older models cannot read text
Rules written by hand will beat any learned model at this task
Sorting emails is a job for an AI agent that plans its own steps

questions.explanation: Assigning one of a few fixed labels is a classic predictive machine learning task, and a trained classifier is often cheaper, faster and more consistent at this scale. Generative AI can classify too, but it is not required, and nothing here calls for an agent that plans steps. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A leader says: 'Generative AI understands our customers, so we can let it decide refunds.' What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: It predicts plausible text; it has no grasp of customers or policy
Refund decisions involve numbers, which language models cannot read
Generative AI is too slow to handle refund requests at any scale
Customers refuse to accept decisions that are made by software

questions.explanation: An LLM predicts plausible text from patterns in data. Fluent output can look like understanding, but the model has no grasp of the customer or of policy, so consequential decisions need grounding, rules and human accountability. Speed is not the issue, and models can read numbers even when they calculate badly. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which task plays to the strengths of generative AI?

options.text: Drafting three product descriptions for a person to edit
Deciding alone which loan applicants are approved or refused
Storing the master record of each customer's contract terms
Calculating the exact payroll tax for each employee every month

questions.explanation: Generative AI is strong at producing drafts and variations that a person then reviews. Exact calculations belong to deterministic software, a system of record must store facts reliably, and consequential decisions such as loan approval need accountability that a model cannot carry. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How do artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning relate to each other?

options.text: AI is a kind of machine learning that has been trained on more data
Machine learning is part of deep learning, which is part of AI
They are three separate fields that happen to share the same tools
Deep learning is part of machine learning, which is part of AI

questions.explanation: AI is the broad field; machine learning is the part of it in which systems learn from data; deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks, which underlie today's LLMs. The reversed nesting is the usual mistake. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What are the parameters of a model?

options.text: The settings a user types into the prompt before each request
The internal values learned in training that shape its outputs
The limits a vendor sets on how many requests a customer can make
The rows of example data that the model was trained on

questions.explanation: Parameters, also called weights, are the numbers a model adjusts during training; model size is often quoted as a parameter count. Settings such as temperature are chosen per request, and training data is the input to learning, not its result. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Pellow Outdoor trains a model on past orders already marked as returned or kept, so it can predict returns. What kind of learning is this?

options.text: Supervised learning
Transfer of rules
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning

questions.explanation: Training on examples that carry the right answer, here returned or kept, is supervised learning. Unsupervised learning finds structure such as clusters in data with no labels, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards for actions taken over time. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A marketing team wants to group customers by buying behaviour, with no categories given in advance. Which technique fits?

options.text: Text generation with a language model
Classification with supervised learning
Clustering with unsupervised learning
Routing with fixed if-then thresholds

questions.explanation: Finding groups in data without predefined labels is clustering, an unsupervised technique. Classification needs labelled examples of each category, which the team does not have, and generating text does not group anything. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is natural language processing (NLP)?

options.text: Translating code from one programming language into another
A method of compressing documents so that they need less storage
A programming language designed for writing AI models
The field of AI that works with human language in text or speech

questions.explanation: NLP covers tasks such as translation, sentiment analysis, summarisation and question answering over human language, and LLMs are its leading technology today. It is not a programming language, although the shared word often misleads. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A vendor calls its product 'AI-powered', yet it applies a fixed set of if-then rules written by staff. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is generative AI, since it produces a decision as its output
It is rule-based automation and learns nothing from data
It is an AI agent, since it acts without a person each time
It is machine learning, since its rules came from human experience

questions.explanation: Hand-written if-then rules are rule-based automation: useful, but the system does not learn from data. Producing an output does not make a system generative, and acting automatically on fixed rules is not the planning and tool use that define an agent. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a token in an LLM?

options.text: A unit of payment that buys one request to the model
One complete sentence of the prompt or of the answer
A password that grants a user access to the model
A small piece of text, often part of a word

questions.explanation: Models process text as tokens, which are often word pieces; a rough guide is about four characters of English per token. Usage is often billed per token, which makes the payment option tempting, but the token itself is a piece of text. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team pastes a 400-page manual into a chat and the model ignores the early chapters. Which limit is the most likely cause?

options.text: The parameter count
The training cut-off
The context window
The temperature setting

questions.explanation: The context window is the most text, counted in tokens, that a model can consider at once; input beyond it is cut off or poorly used. Retrieval, which sends only the relevant passages, is the usual remedy. The training cut-off limits what the model learned, not what it can read now. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is an embedding?

options.text: A hidden watermark that marks text as written by AI
A model that has been installed inside another application
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of some content
A short summary that is attached to the top of a long document

questions.explanation: An embedding turns text, images or other content into a vector of numbers so that similar meanings sit close together; RAG uses embeddings to find relevant passages. Installing a model inside an app is a different, everyday use of the word. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An assistant's answer quotes the policy document it was given and stays within it. Which term describes this answer?

options.text: Multimodal
Grounded
Hallucinated
Fine-tuned

questions.explanation: Output is grounded when it rests on supplied source material, such as retrieved documents, rather than on the model's general training. Fine-tuning changes the model itself, and hallucination is the opposite of grounding: fluent content with no support. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Two prompts to the same model differ only in their system message. Why can the answers differ sharply?

options.text: The system message switches the request to a different model
The system message changes the data the model was trained on
The system message is ignored, so any difference is random
The system message frames the role, rules and tone throughout

questions.explanation: A system message frames everything that follows: who the assistant is, what it must and must not do, and how to respond. It does not change the model or its training data, and models do follow it, although not perfectly. Topic 1.3, lesson “1.1-1.3 · Generative AI, LLMs and the core vocabulary”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Prompt engineering techniques.

questions.prompt: Mirren Insurance adds a model that reads scanned claim forms and extracts the fields, while the rest of the flow stays a fixed sequence of steps. Which level of AI fits best?

options.text: Intelligent Automation
Agentic Workflows
Rule-Based Automation
Full-Autonomous Agents

questions.explanation: A fixed process with an AI component, here reading documents, matches Intelligent Automation, the second level. Nothing plans or chooses steps, so it is not yet agentic. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A process runs a set sequence of steps, but at two points an LLM decides which branch to take and drafts the content for it. Which level of AI fits best?

options.text: Agentic Workflows
Rule-Based Automation
Semi-Automatic Agents
Full-Autonomous Agents

questions.explanation: In an agentic workflow, people design the overall flow and AI makes decisions and does work inside it. An agent at the two higher levels would plan its own sequence of steps toward a goal instead of following a designed path. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What changes from one level to the next as the five levels of AI rise from Rule-Based Automation to Full-Autonomous Agents?

options.text: Each level uses a newer and larger language model
Each level removes another team from the process
Each level costs less to run than the one beneath it
More of the decisions and actions pass to the AI

questions.explanation: The ladder runs from fixed rules to agents that act unsupervised, so autonomy rises at each step and so does the need for governance. The levels describe who decides and acts, not the size of the model or its running cost. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Corwen Logistics lets an agent reorder stock and agree delivery slots with suppliers' systems, with no person approving any step. Which level of AI is this?

options.text: Agentic Workflows
Intelligent Automation
Semi-Automatic Agents
Full-Autonomous Agents

questions.explanation: Planning and acting with no approval step is the top level. If a buyer had to approve each order before it was placed, the same agent would sit at Semi-Automatic Agents. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Intelligent Automation and a Full-Autonomous Agent would both meet a team's need. Which choice is wiser, and why?

options.text: Either, since Intelligent Automation and agents carry equal risk
The agent, since full autonomy gives the best results
Intelligent Automation, as less autonomy means less to govern
The agent, since it removes the human cost of the task

questions.explanation: Choose the lowest level that solves the problem: each step up gives the AI more freedom to act, which raises the cost of testing, monitoring and accountability. A higher level is not automatically better. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the level of AI it best illustrates.

options.text: Rule-Based Automation
Agentic Workflows
Intelligent Automation
Semi-Automatic Agents
Full-Autonomous Agents

slots.text: An if-then script approves invoices that match the order
A fixed flow uses a model to read scanned forms
An agent plans the work and waits for approval before acting
An agent plans and acts with no approval step

questions.explanation: The examples climb the ladder: fixed rules, a fixed flow with an AI component, an agent that needs approval, and an agent that acts alone. Agentic Workflows, where AI makes choices inside a designed flow, matches none of them. The outline only names the five levels; their full definitions are taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 1.4, lesson “1.4 · The five levels of AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In a RAG solution, what is a vector index used for?

options.text: Storing the model's weights after each fine-tuning run
Finding passages whose meaning is close to the question
Encrypting each prompt before it is sent on to the model
Counting how many tokens each request will consume

questions.explanation: Documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings and stored in an index; at question time the question is embedded too and the nearest chunks are retrieved. The index holds content, not model weights, which is why RAG works without retraining. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: Brightwell Council's RAG assistant still answers from the 2019 parking rules after the 2026 rules were published. What should be fixed first?

options.text: Move to a model with a larger context window
Raise the temperature so that its answers vary more
Refresh the index with the current documents
Fine-tune the model on the new 2026 parking rules

questions.explanation: A RAG system can only ground answers in what its index contains, so stale or duplicate documents produce stale answers; the fix is to update the content and how it is ingested. Fine-tuning is slower and would bake in rules that will change again. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: Retrieval for a contract assistant returns long chunks in which the relevant clause is buried among unrelated text, and answers are often vague. Which change is most likely to help?

options.text: Retrieve twice as many chunks for each question
Split documents into smaller, coherent chunks
Send each contract in full with every request
Replace retrieval with a single fine-tuned model

questions.explanation: Chunking strongly affects retrieval: chunks that are too large dilute the relevant clause, while chunks that are too small lose context. Retrieving more of the same long chunks adds noise, and sending each contract in full runs into the context window and cost. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which need points to RAG rather than to fine-tuning?

options.text: Replies must follow a house style across thousands of messages
Outputs must follow a fixed format learned from many examples
The model must respond faster on a narrow, repeated task
Answers must cite the current version of internal documents

questions.explanation: RAG suits knowledge that changes and answers that must show their source. Fine-tuning suits behaviour, such as style, format or narrow-task performance, which is why it fits the other three needs better. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps that prepare documents for retrieval in a RAG solution.

options.text: Split them into chunks
Create an embedding for each chunk
Store the chunks and embeddings in an index
Collect the source documents

questions.explanation: Ingestion runs collect, chunk, embed and index; only then can questions be matched against the content. Embedding comes after chunking because each chunk gets its own vector. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes.

questions.prompt: A RAG assistant answers well in testing but shows salary figures to staff who should not see them. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The temperature is set too high for confidential topics
The vendor trained the model on the salary data
The context window is too small to hold the access rules
Retrieval ignores each user's access rights

questions.explanation: RAG brings documents into the prompt, so retrieval must respect the same access rights as the source system; otherwise any user can surface any indexed document. The vendor never saw the salary files, and temperature has no bearing on who can see what. Topic 1.5, lesson “1.5 · Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does composite AI often give more robust results than a single technique?

options.text: It uses one very large model trained on far more data
It runs one model several times and keeps the longest answer
It needs no data, because rules make the decisions
Each method handles the part of the problem it does best

questions.explanation: The study guide describes composite AI as combining machine learning, rules-based systems and LLMs for more accurate and robust results than one method alone. Rules give certainty where policy is fixed, machine learning predicts from data, and LLMs handle language. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations.

questions.prompt: A mortgage assistant must apply legal lending limits exactly, estimate default risk from past loans, and explain the outcome to the applicant in plain words. Which design fits?

options.text: A risk model for the limits and the default risk, an LLM to explain
Rules for the limits, a risk model for default, an LLM to explain
An LLM for the limits, the risk estimate and the words that explain it
Rules for the limits and the risk, a template to explain each outcome

questions.explanation: This is composite AI: deterministic rules for limits that must hold exactly, machine learning for a risk estimate from history, and an LLM for clear language. Handing the legal limits to a model, an LLM or a risk model, loses the exactness of rules, and fixed rules cannot learn default risk from past loans. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In a composite design, an LLM proposes a discount and a rule caps any discount at 15 percent. What does the rule add?

options.text: Better wording in the message that goes to the customer
A way for the model to learn from each discount it offers
A hard limit that holds whatever the model suggests
A faster reply, since rules run before the model is called

questions.explanation: Rules are predictable and auditable, so they enforce limits that a probabilistic model might break. The rule does not improve wording or teach the model anything; it constrains the output. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which system is an example of composite AI?

options.text: An image generator creates a new banner from a text prompt each day
A classifier routes tickets, rules set deadlines, an LLM drafts replies
One large language model answers every question in the customer support chat
A macro copies ticket totals into a report at the end of each month

questions.explanation: Composite AI combines different techniques in one solution: here a learned classifier, fixed rules and an LLM. A single model, however capable, is not composite, and a macro involves no AI at all. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team proposes to replace its fixed tax rules with an LLM 'because AI is smarter'. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: Rules are a newer technology than language models are
Tax logic must be exact and auditable, which suits rules
Language models cannot process tables of figures in any format
Language models need internet access to work out tax amounts

questions.explanation: Where logic is fixed and must be exact and auditable, rules beat a probabilistic model; the composite approach keeps them and uses AI where learning or language adds value. Models can read tables, but reading is not the same as applying policy reliably. Topic 1.6, lesson “1.6 · Composite AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does tool use mean for an AI agent?

options.text: Installing the model on a laptop so that it runs offline
Switching between languages when it translates an answer
Choosing which prompt template to show the user on screen
Calling functions or APIs to fetch data or to act

questions.explanation: Tools are the functions, APIs and services an agent can call, such as search, a database query or sending an email, and they let it act beyond producing text. Each tool also widens what can go wrong, which is why tool permissions matter. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: What is the role of memory in an AI agent?

options.text: Keeping state so that later steps build on earlier ones
Recording each user's password so that it can sign in for them
Holding the API keys the agent needs to call its tools
Storing a copy of the model's weights in case the vendor changes them

questions.explanation: Memory lets an agent keep track of what it has done, what tools returned and what the user said, within a task or across sessions. Credentials belong in a secure store with tightly scoped permissions, not in agent memory. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Source: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption.

questions.prompt: An agent asked to book a team offsite searches venues, finds the first choice full, picks another and emails the team. Which capability does the change of venue show?

options.text: Following a fixed script written in advance
Retraining itself on the venue's past booking data
Adjusting its plan based on what a tool returned
Generating an image of the venue for the email

questions.explanation: Agents loop through plan, act and observe: a tool result, here a full venue, changes the next step. A fixed script cannot adapt like this, and nothing in the task involves retraining. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which use case benefits most from an AI agent rather than a single LLM call?

options.text: Rewriting a paragraph of the monthly newsletter in a friendlier tone
Summarising a single meeting transcript for the team
Translating a product description from English into French
A billing query that needs the account, the invoice and a refund

questions.explanation: Agents earn their extra complexity on multi-step tasks that need data from several systems and an action at the end. Rewriting, translating and summarising one supplied text need no tools or planning, so a single prompt is proportionate. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An agent sometimes loops, calling the same search tool dozens of times without finishing. Which safeguard addresses this most directly?

options.text: A cap on steps or tool calls, with a hand-off to a person
A larger context window so that it remembers more searches
A higher temperature so that it tries more varied searches
A longer system prompt about the company's history

questions.explanation: Agents need run-time limits such as maximum steps, time or cost, plus a defined escalation when a limit is reached. More context or more randomness does not stop a loop, and background history does nothing for control. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each agent capability to an example of it.

options.text: Recalling the dietary needs the user gave last week
Choosing a larger model for the next request
Checking the draft itinerary against the budget before sending it
Querying the booking system for free rooms
Breaking 'organise the offsite' into venue, budget and invitations

questions.explanation: Planning breaks a goal into steps, tool use reaches outside systems, memory keeps context over time, and reflection checks work before acting on it. Together they make an agent more than a single model call. Topic 1.7, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a plain LLM that has no tools?

options.text: It turns a prompt into text and takes no action in other systems
It carries out tasks in business systems once it is given a goal
It browses the web for fresh facts before it answers a question
It keeps learning from each conversation and updates its weights

questions.explanation: On its own an LLM maps input text to output text; it does not act, browse or learn between conversations. Those abilities come from the system built around it, such as tools, retrieval and memory, which is what an agent adds. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A help desk wants software that resets passwords, checks the ticket queue and updates the ticket when done. What does it need beyond an LLM?

options.text: A larger model trained on more ticket transcripts
Tool access to the identity and ticket systems
A higher temperature so that it responds more naturally
A longer prompt that explains the reset procedure

questions.explanation: Acting in systems needs tools and an agent loop that decides when to call them; the model alone can only describe the steps. A bigger model or a longer prompt improves text, not the ability to act. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A manager asks whether a new tool should be called 'an agent'. It drafts emails from a prompt, and a person reads and sends them. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: It is an agent, since it writes emails without being edited
It is an agent, since it uses a language model for its output
It is an agent, since a person is involved in the process
It is an LLM application: it neither plans steps nor acts

questions.explanation: Drafting text for a person to send is a plain LLM use, because the person does the acting. An agent would decide on steps and use tools, for example finding the recipient's history and sending the message itself. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly contrasts an LLM with an AI agent?

options.text: LLM: calls tools to act. Agent: writes text in reply to a prompt
LLM: learns from each chat. Agent: follows a fixed set of rules
LLM: runs with no prompt. Agent: needs a detailed prompt each time
LLM: responds to a prompt. Agent: pursues a goal using tools

questions.explanation: The core difference is goal-directed action: an LLM produces a response, while an agent uses a model to plan and call tools toward a goal. The reversed pair is the trap, along with the belief that LLMs learn from each chat. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team gives its chatbot a tool that looks up order status. A customer then asks it to cancel an order. What can the chatbot do?

options.text: Cancel the order, since an LLM can act on what the user asks
Cancel the order, since it can already reach the order system
Refuse to discuss the order, since cancelling needs an agent
Explain how to cancel, since none of its tools cancels

questions.explanation: An LLM-based assistant can act only through the tools it is given, and a read-only status tool cannot cancel anything. That is also a security property: limiting tools limits what an assistant can do if it is misled. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When is a single LLM call, rather than an agent, the better design?

options.text: When the task spans several systems and ends with a record update
When work must continue overnight with nobody present
When it is one step on supplied input, with a person reviewing
When the system must choose its own next step each time

questions.explanation: Simpler designs are easier to test, cheaper and safer, so a single model call is preferred when no tools, planning or autonomy are needed. The other three conditions describe exactly the cases where an agent earns its extra complexity. Topic 1.8, lesson “1.7-1.8 · AI agents and how they differ from an LLM”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does an agentic AI approach mean?

options.text: Giving AI a goal and letting it plan and act within set limits
Replacing manual processes with fixed scripts and if-then rules
Using AI to answer questions that people type into a chat window
Training a new model from scratch for each business process

questions.explanation: Agentic AI moves from asking a model for an answer to assigning it an outcome: it plans steps, uses tools, checks results and adapts, inside boundaries that people set. Answering typed questions is the chat pattern, and fixed scripts are rule-based automation. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a multi-agent system?

options.text: Specialised agents that pass work to each other toward one goal
One agent copied onto many servers to handle more users
A group of people who each review the same model output
A single model that is asked the same question several times over

questions.explanation: In a multi-agent system, agents with distinct roles, such as a researcher, a writer and a reviewer, coordinate, often under an orchestrator. Running copies of one agent for scale is just deployment, not a multi-agent design. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A design has a planner agent that splits a request into tasks and assigns them to a research agent and a drafting agent. What is the planner's role called?

options.text: Embedding model
Orchestrator
Guardrail
Retriever

questions.explanation: An orchestrator coordinates other agents: it breaks down the work, routes tasks and combines the results. A retriever finds content for grounding, and a guardrail checks or blocks inputs and outputs. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In an agentic process for onboarding new suppliers, where does a human-in-the-loop step belong?

options.text: Nowhere, since an approval step defeats the point of agents
After onboarding, in a review that is held once a year
Before each web search the agent runs to gather supplier details
Before the agent signs or commits to anything for the company

questions.explanation: Human approval is placed at points of consequence, such as contracts, payments and irreversible changes, so that oversight is meaningful without slowing each low-risk step. Approving every search makes reviewers a bottleneck and soon a rubber stamp. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An agent runs a 30-step task overnight, and in the morning nobody can say why it emailed a supplier. What was missing?

options.text: Traces of each step, tool call and reason
A larger model with more parameters
A shorter context window to keep it focused
A higher temperature for more creative steps

questions.explanation: Observability, meaning logs and traces of the agent's plan, tool calls and results, is what lets people audit, debug and stay accountable for autonomous work. Without it, even a correct action cannot be explained. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which is a guardrail in an agentic system?

options.text: Refunds above a set amount wait for a person to approve
A larger budget for the tokens the agent can use each day
A prompt asking the agent to try its very best on each task
A dashboard showing how many tasks it finished last month

questions.explanation: Guardrails are controls that constrain what an agent can do or say, such as limits, allow-lists, content filters and approval gates. Encouraging wording is not a control, and a monthly dashboard only reports after the fact. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company wants to adopt agentic AI. Which first project is most sensible?

options.text: A company-wide agent that can act in many systems at once
A customer-facing agent that can issue refunds with no limit
A bounded, reversible internal task with clear measures
A project picked because a competitor announced one

questions.explanation: Start where errors are cheap and visible: bounded scope, reversible actions, clear measures and internal users. That builds evidence and governance habits before agents act for customers or across many systems. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An agentic design uses a reviewer agent to check a writer agent's report against the source data before it goes out. Which practice is this?

options.text: Prompt injection testing of the writer
Automated checking of agent output
Fine-tuning of the writer agent
Data minimisation in the report

questions.explanation: A common agentic pattern pairs a generating agent with a checking agent, a form of reflection that catches errors before people see them. It reduces risk but does not replace human accountability for consequential output. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement about autonomy in agentic AI is most accurate?

options.text: Autonomy matters for customer-facing agents and few others
Autonomy is set by the model vendor and cannot be changed
Autonomy should be at its maximum at launch to show value
Autonomy should grow as evidence of reliable results grows

questions.explanation: Teams usually start agents with tight limits and human approval, then widen their freedom as monitoring shows reliable behaviour, much like moving up the five levels. Autonomy is a design choice made by the team, not a property fixed by the vendor. Topic 1.9, lesson “1.9 · The agentic AI approach”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which three things are usually configured when building a custom GPT?

options.text: Servers, databases and network rules
Weights, training data and GPU hardware
Instructions, knowledge files and actions
Tokens, temperature and the context window

questions.explanation: A custom GPT is configured, not trained: instructions set its behaviour, knowledge files give it material to draw on, and actions connect it to outside APIs. Changing weights or training data would be fine-tuning, which a custom GPT does not involve. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Ardley Consulting builds a custom GPT for writing proposals and uploads its internal rate card. Which risk should it check before sharing the GPT with clients?

options.text: The GPT will forget the rate card after about a week
Clients cannot use a GPT unless they pay for training
Users may draw out the uploaded file's content
The GPT cannot read the numbers in an uploaded file

questions.explanation: Knowledge files can often be surfaced by asking the GPT about them, so confidential material should not be uploaded to an assistant that outsiders can use. Uploaded files do not expire after a week, and reading numbers is not the problem. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a copilot built into an office suite from a standalone chatbot?

options.text: It works inside the user's own apps and files
It uses no language model, just fixed rules
It acts alone, without the user seeing its work
It needs a programming background to use

questions.explanation: A copilot sits inside the application where the work happens, drawing on the user's documents, mail or code, and offers suggestions the user accepts or edits. It keeps the person in control, which is the opposite of acting alone. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A sales team wants a reusable assistant that checks draft proposals against its pricing rules and writes a summary for approvers. It changes nothing in any system. Which option is most proportionate?

options.text: A multi-agent system with an orchestrator and five agents
A fully autonomous agent that sends proposals to clients
A custom GPT whose instructions hold the price policy
A model trained from scratch on past proposals

questions.explanation: A configured assistant with instructions and reference files is the lightest option that meets the need, and it needs no tools because nothing in a system changes. Autonomous sending removes the approvers, and training a model from scratch is far beyond what the task needs. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why test a custom GPT with awkward and off-topic requests before sharing it?

options.text: To confirm that its knowledge files have been encrypted
To see if it stays in its role when users push it
To make the GPT learn the right answers to those requests
To lower the cost of each conversation that it handles

questions.explanation: Instructions are guidance that a model follows imperfectly, so builders test edge cases and adversarial requests to see whether the GPT refuses, escalates or stays on task. Testing teaches the GPT nothing; changing its instructions or files is what changes its behaviour. Topic 1.10, lesson “1.10 · Custom GPTs and copilots”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A hiring model recommends equally qualified candidates at different rates depending on their gender. Which responsible AI principle is most directly breached?

options.text: Accountability
Fairness
Transparency
Reliability

questions.explanation: Fairness means similar people receive similar outcomes, without unfair treatment tied to sensitive attributes. Transparency would be the issue if candidates were not told how AI was used, which is a different problem from unequal outcomes. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Responsible AI for agent design.

questions.prompt: A bank's chatbot introduces itself as a human adviser and gives no sign that its answers are generated. Which principle is most directly breached?

options.text: Transparency
Inclusiveness
Reliability
Fairness

questions.explanation: Transparency means people can see that AI is involved and understand its capabilities and limits. The answers may be perfectly fair and reliable, yet customers are still misled about what they are talking to. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Responsible AI for agent design.

questions.prompt: After an AI pricing tool overcharges customers, each department says the model made the decision and that nobody owns it. Which principle is missing?

options.text: Transparency
Accountability
Fairness
Privacy

questions.explanation: Accountability means named people remain answerable for an AI system and its outcomes. Transparency is tempting, but the problem is not that the decision is hidden; it is that nobody takes responsibility for it. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Source: Microsoft Learn · Responsible AI for agent design.

questions.prompt: Which GDPR principle says to collect only the personal data needed for the stated purpose?

options.text: Storage limitation
Purpose limitation
Data minimisation
Integrity and confidentiality

questions.explanation: Data minimisation limits collection to what is necessary. Purpose limitation is the close neighbour: it is about not reusing data for incompatible purposes, not about how much is collected. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Article 5 · Principles.

questions.prompt: Support transcripts with customer names were collected lawfully and are used solely for support, but the company has no deletion schedule and keeps them forever. Which GDPR principle does this most directly conflict with?

options.text: Purpose limitation
Storage limitation
Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
Accuracy

questions.explanation: Storage limitation says personal data is kept no longer than needed. Purpose limitation is the tempting answer, but the purpose has not changed here; only the retention period is unbounded. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Article 5 · Principles.

questions.prompt: A company based in Singapore, with no office in Europe, sells subscriptions to consumers in France and processes their personal data. Does the GDPR apply?

options.text: No, since the company has no establishment inside the EU
No, since its servers are located outside European territory
Yes, but only where a customer holds an EU passport
Yes, since it offers services to people who are in the EU

questions.explanation: Article 3 extends the GDPR to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the Union. Having no EU establishment is the tempting reason to say no, and it is exactly the case the article covers. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Article 3 · Territorial scope.

questions.prompt: How does the GDPR treat pseudonymised data that could be linked back to a person with a separately kept key?

options.text: As anonymous information that is outside its scope
As personal data that remains within its scope
As special category data that cannot be processed
As public data that any person is free to reuse

questions.explanation: Recital 26 says pseudonymised data that can be attributed to a person with additional information is still personal data. Only information that no longer identifies anyone counts as anonymous and falls outside the rules. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Recital 26 · Anonymous and pseudonymised data; GDPR Article 4 · Definitions.

questions.prompt: A data team wants to train a model on support tickets with no GDPR obligations attached to the training set. What must be true of that data?

options.text: People cannot be identified from it by reasonably likely means
Each email address is hashed together with a secret salt value
Names are replaced by codes and the lookup table is locked away
All tickets are encrypted while they are stored and transferred

questions.explanation: Only anonymous information, where people are no longer identifiable, is outside the GDPR. Replacing names with codes while keeping the lookup table is pseudonymisation, and that data is still personal data. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Recital 26 · Anonymous and pseudonymised data.

questions.prompt: Which GDPR right lets a person ask a company to delete their personal data on certain grounds?

options.text: The right to data portability
The right to erasure
The right to rectification
The right to object

questions.explanation: Article 17 sets out the right to erasure, also known as the right to be forgotten. Rectification is about correcting inaccurate data, so the data stays; erasure removes it. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Article 17 · Right to erasure.

questions.prompt: Which situation falls under the GDPR right concerning decisions based solely on automated processing?

options.text: A loan refused by an algorithm with no human involved
A clerk who totals an invoice using a spreadsheet
A chatbot that suggests help articles to a site visitor
A spam filter that moves a newsletter to a folder

questions.explanation: Article 22 covers decisions made solely by automated means that have legal or similarly significant effects on a person, such as refusing credit. A spam filter is automated too, but its effect on the person is not significant in that sense. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Source: GDPR Article 22 · Automated individual decision-making.

questions.prompt: Whose personal information does the California Consumer Privacy Act protect?

options.text: Citizens of any US state
Businesses registered in California
Residents of California
Residents of the European Union

questions.explanation: The CCPA gives privacy rights to California residents. It is a state law, so it does not protect residents of other states, and the European equivalent is the GDPR. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A California customer tells a retailer to stop passing their personal information to data brokers for money. Which CCPA right are they using?

options.text: The right to know what is being collected
The right to correct inaccurate information
The right to equal service and pricing
The right to opt out of sale or sharing

questions.explanation: The CCPA lets consumers opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information. The right to know is about finding out what a business holds and does; it does not by itself stop the selling. Topic 2.4, lesson “2.4 · Data privacy: governance, anonymisation, GDPR and CCPA”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An assistant that summarises web pages reads hidden text on a page telling it to forward the user's emails, and it tries to comply. What is this attack called?

options.text: Indirect prompt injection
Direct prompt injection
Model inversion
Training data poisoning

questions.explanation: The malicious instruction arrived inside external content the model processed, which makes it indirect prompt injection. In a direct injection the attacker types the instruction into the prompt personally. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · AI security: dos and don'ts”. Source: OWASP GenAI · LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection.

questions.prompt: An agent that only has to read order status has been given an API key that can also issue refunds. Which fix addresses the risk most directly?

options.text: Move the agent to a larger and more recent model
Add several refund examples to its instructions
Raise the temperature so that its choices are varied
Limit the key to the permissions that the task needs

questions.explanation: Excessive permissions are a root cause of excessive agency, and the fix is least privilege for each tool. A better model does not help: any model can be manipulated or mistaken, and then the spare permission is what does the damage. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · AI security: dos and don'ts”. Source: OWASP GenAI · LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency.

questions.prompt: An agent can draft and send payments. Which control best balances usefulness with safety?

options.text: The agent approves payments by its own judgement
A person approves each payment before it is sent
The prompt asks the model to be careful with money
Logging is switched off so amounts stay private

questions.explanation: High-impact, hard-to-reverse actions such as payments call for a human approval gate. An instruction in the prompt to be careful is the tempting shortcut, but instructions can be overridden by manipulated input, whereas an approval step cannot. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · AI security: dos and don'ts”. Source: OWASP GenAI · LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency; Microsoft Learn · AI agent shared responsibility model.

questions.prompt: An analyst wants to paste a customer list with names and account numbers into a free public chatbot to tidy it up. What is the responsible course?

options.text: Use an approved tool or remove the personal data first
Paste the list and delete the chat history afterwards
Paste half of the list so that less data is exposed
Ask the chatbot to confirm that it will forget the data

questions.explanation: Personal and confidential data should go only into tools the organisation has approved, or be removed before use. Deleting the chat afterwards does not undo the disclosure, because the data has already left the company's control. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · AI security: dos and don'ts”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each function of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework to its description.

options.text: Establishes the context in which risks are framed
Certifies that a model is free of bias
Allocates resources to respond to the risks
Builds the culture, policies and accountability for AI risk
Analyses, assesses and monitors the risks

questions.explanation: The framework has four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. Govern is the cross-cutting one that runs through the other three, and map and measure are the pair most often swapped: map frames the risks, measure assesses them. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Ethical decision-making frameworks for AI”. Source: NIST AI RMF 1.0 · Core functions.

questions.prompt: A team is unsure whether an AI feature that predicts which employees may resign is appropriate. Which step belongs earliest in an ethical review?

options.text: Measure the accuracy of the model on held-out data
Identify who is affected and how they could be harmed
Write the launch announcement for the affected staff
Choose the vendor with the lowest cost per prediction

questions.explanation: Ethical review starts with the people affected and the possible harms, before any decision to build. Accuracy matters later, but an accurate model can still be the wrong thing to deploy. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Ethical decision-making frameworks for AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes explainability in responsible AI?

options.text: The system's source code is published for anyone to read
Every output is labelled with the name of the model used
Users receive a printed manual describing the model's features
People can understand why the system produced a given output

questions.explanation: Explainability means the reasons behind an output can be understood well enough to check, challenge or act on it, for example the main factors behind a credit decision. Publishing code or naming the model is transparency about the system, which helps but explains no single decision. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A recruiting model was trained on ten years of hiring decisions in which few women were hired into engineering roles. Which risk does this create most directly?

options.text: The model declines to rank candidates of any kind
The model runs too slowly on long candidate lists
The model leaks the names of earlier candidates
The model learns and repeats the historical bias

questions.explanation: A model trained on biased decisions treats them as the pattern to copy, so unfair outcomes are reproduced at scale; this is why training data is examined for representation and outcomes are tested across groups. Speed and refusals are not what the history causes. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice best supports fairness before an AI model is released?

options.text: Withholding its documentation so it cannot be gamed
Raising its accuracy on the largest group of users
Comparing its error rates across different groups of users
Letting it learn freely from live user feedback straight away

questions.explanation: Fairness testing compares outcomes and error rates across groups, because a model can be accurate on average while failing one group badly. Optimising for the majority can hide exactly that gap. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does accountability mean for an AI system?

options.text: Named people answer for its outcomes and can change or stop it
The system's users accept the risk when they agree to the terms
The model keeps a log of its own decisions for later review
The vendor of the model is liable for each output it produces

questions.explanation: Accountability means a person or role owns the system's outcomes, with the authority to intervene. Logs support accountability but do not provide it, and an organisation cannot hand responsibility for its use of AI to a vendor or to its users. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An insurer's model sets premiums, and customers ask why theirs rose. Staff can say only that 'the system decided'. Which principle is weakest here?

options.text: Storage limitation
Data minimisation
Inclusiveness
Explainability

questions.explanation: When nobody can give the reasons for an individual outcome, the system fails on explainability, and accountability suffers with it. Data minimisation and storage limitation concern which personal data is kept and for how long. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A voice assistant works well for most users but often fails for people with strong regional accents. Which principle does this raise?

options.text: Transparency
Accountability
Data minimisation
Inclusiveness

questions.explanation: Inclusiveness asks whether a system works for the full range of people who will use it, including those with different accents, abilities or languages. The fix starts with more representative data and testing with those users. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team argues that its model is fair because gender is not one of its inputs. Why can this argument fail?

options.text: Gender has to be included for the model to work as designed
Other inputs, such as job titles or postcodes, can act as proxies
Fairness depends mostly on how quickly the model returns an answer
Removing inputs makes a model less transparent to its users

questions.explanation: Dropping a protected attribute does not stop a model from learning it through correlated features, so outcomes can still differ by gender. Fairness is checked by measuring outcomes across groups, not by inspecting the input list. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which disclosure best supports transparency for a customer-facing chatbot?

options.text: Listing the vendors whose servers host the chatbot
Showing the chatbot's response time beside each reply
Publishing the parameter count of the underlying model
Telling users it is AI and what it can and cannot do

questions.explanation: Transparency to users means they know they are dealing with AI, what it is for and its limits, so they can judge its output and ask for a person when needed. Technical facts such as parameter counts tell a customer nothing useful. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A model that triages patient messages is 95 percent accurate overall. Which further fact matters most before deciding whether it is responsible to use?

options.text: How many parameters the underlying model has
Whether it answers faster than the nurses do now
Which programming language the system is written in
What it gets wrong, and how often for urgent cases

questions.explanation: An average hides the cost of errors: missing an urgent case is far worse than misrouting a routine one, so error types and rates for high-risk cases decide whether the system is safe. Speed and implementation details come later. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a model card?

options.text: A diagram showing the layers inside the model's neural network
A document of a model's intended use, limits and test results
A summary of what the model costs to run each month
A licence key that unlocks the model for one named user

questions.explanation: Model cards record what a model is for, how it was trained and evaluated, where it performs poorly and what it should not be used for. They support transparency and help users decide whether a model fits their context. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI tool flags employees for possible misconduct. Which design choice best protects the people affected?

options.text: Flags go straight to managers so that action is taken quickly
The tool's scores are kept secret to prevent gaming
Flagged employees are suspended while the tool learns
A person reviews each flag, and employees can contest it

questions.explanation: For consequential decisions about people, human review and a route to challenge the outcome are basic safeguards. Speed and secrecy serve the organisation rather than the person flagged, and acting on an unreviewed flag punishes possible errors. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI feature summarises customer complaints for managers. Which practice keeps it reliable and safe after launch?

options.text: Asking customers about problems in an annual survey
Monitoring its outputs and reviewing a sample regularly
Switching to the newest model as soon as one appears
Testing it once before launch and then leaving it alone

questions.explanation: Model behaviour drifts as inputs and models change, so reliability needs ongoing monitoring, sampling and a way to act on problems. A one-off test or a yearly survey finds issues long after they have caused harm. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of a responsible AI principle with a practice is correct?

options.text: Privacy: share the training data with all employees
Transparency: encrypt each prompt the system stores
Fairness: test outcomes across groups of users
Accountability: let the model approve its own changes

questions.explanation: Fairness is shown by comparing outcomes across groups. Encryption serves security and privacy rather than transparency; a model approving its own changes removes accountability; and sharing personal training data widely works against privacy. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · Principles of responsible AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question is at the heart of an AI impact assessment?

options.text: How quickly can the system be put into production next quarter?
Which team will own the system's cloud budget next year?
Who could this system affect, and how could they be harmed?
Which vendor offers the lowest price per thousand tokens?

questions.explanation: An impact assessment looks at the people and groups a system touches, the harms it could cause and how likely and severe they are, so that mitigations, or a decision not to proceed, come before launch. Cost, speed and budget ownership matter, but they are not ethical questions. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2 · Ethical decision-making frameworks for AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team could build a model that infers which customers are pregnant from their purchases, to target offers. Which ethical question should come first?

options.text: Should this be done, given how customers would see it?
Which model would predict pregnancy most accurately?
How soon can the offers reach the customers who are involved?
Which channel gives the offers the highest response?

questions.explanation: Ethical frameworks put 'should we' before 'can we': inferring sensitive facts that customers never shared can be intrusive and harmful even when legal and accurate.
