Source: Scaled Agile · AI-Native overview.

questions.prompt: A CFO asks why the AI plan is reviewed every quarter rather than once a year. Which EDGE force gives the best reason?

options.text: Exponential: capability and cost change too fast for yearly plans
Generative: AI can draft a whole new plan in a few minutes each time
Emergent: the plan will write itself as the models improve
Disruptive: competitors review their own plans each quarter

questions.explanation: Exponential growth in capability and falling cost per task mean assumptions go stale within months, so plans need short review cycles. The other options misuse the force names. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team is surprised that a model can translate between a pair of languages it was never explicitly trained to pair. How should a leader use this insight?

options.text: Run small experiments, since useful abilities can appear unplanned
Ignore it, since unplanned abilities have no use in business
Retrain the model to remove abilities that nobody designed
Wait for the vendor to publish a complete list of all its abilities

questions.explanation: Emergence means models can show capabilities nobody designed for, so organisations discover value, and risk, by experimenting and testing rather than by reading a specification. Waiting for a complete list misunderstands the force. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team wants AI to draft first versions of meeting summaries, a use that is widely adopted with well-known practices. How should it be classified?

options.text: Emergent
Evolving
Stable
Frontier

questions.explanation: A use with proven patterns, broad adoption and predictable results reads as Stable, so it can be adopted with standard controls. Emergent is one of the EDGE forces, not one of the three classes. The outline names the three classes; their meaning is taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A use case relies on autonomous agents negotiating contracts with each other, with few examples anywhere of this working in production. How should it be classified?

options.text: Exponential
Evolving
Stable
Frontier

questions.explanation: Experimental uses with little evidence of production success and high uncertainty read as Frontier: worth small, time-boxed experiments, not large commitments. The outline names the three classes; their meaning is taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An assistant answers staff questions over the company's own documents. Patterns for it exist, but results vary with data quality and design. Which class fits best?

options.text: Stable
Frontier
Evolving
Generative

questions.explanation: A use with known patterns whose results still depend heavily on data and design reads as Evolving: pilot it, measure it and mature it before scaling. The outline names the three classes; their meaning is taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why classify AI use cases as Stable, Evolving or Frontier before funding them?

options.text: To rank the use cases by how many staff members they would replace
To publish the list of use cases in the annual report
To decide which vendor's model to buy for each use case
To match investment, controls and expectations to the uncertainty

questions.explanation: Classifying by maturity shows where to scale with confidence, where to pilot with care and where to run small, time-boxed experiments, so risk and spending fit the uncertainty. It is not a vendor or headcount ranking. The outline names the three classes; their meaning is taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company's AI portfolio holds Frontier use cases and nothing else. What is the main risk?

options.text: Too little learning about where AI is heading next
Too few risks to justify having AI governance at all
Little dependable value soon, as most bets may fail
Too much spending on tools that are already mature

questions.explanation: A balanced portfolio mixes Stable uses that deliver value now, Evolving uses being matured and a few Frontier bets. Frontier alone means high uncertainty with little near-term return; it gives plenty of learning, not too little. The outline names the three classes; their meaning is taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A use case was Frontier two years ago and is now common, with proven tools and practices. What should the team do with its classification?

options.text: Reclassify it as it matures, and adjust its controls and funding
Move it to Evolving only after a full year of audits
Keep it as Frontier, since a class is set once and then kept for good
Remove it from the portfolio, since it is no longer new

questions.explanation: Classes describe maturity at a point in time, and uses move from Frontier toward Stable as patterns and tools mature, so classification is revisited. Mature uses are often where value is delivered, so dropping them makes no sense. The outline names the three classes; their meaning is taught in the course, so check this reading against your workbook. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.1-4.2 · EDGE, the AI-Native case, and Stable, Evolving, Frontier”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants to forecast weekly demand for each product from three years of sales data. Which solution pattern fits best?

options.text: A custom GPT with instructions
Predictive machine learning
A retrieval-augmented assistant
A generative AI chatbot

questions.explanation: Forecasting numbers from historical data is a predictive machine learning problem. Generative patterns produce content and can explain a forecast, but they are not the right tool for producing it. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A legal team wants help drafting standard letters that a lawyer then edits. Which pattern is the most practical start?

options.text: A prompt-based assistant with templates and examples
An autonomous agent that sends letters to clients
A model fine-tuned on every letter the firm has sent
A predictive model that scores each letter's risk

questions.explanation: When the task is drafting with a person reviewing, a well-prompted assistant with examples is the lightest pattern that works; fine-tuning is worth considering only if prompting falls short at scale. Sending letters autonomously removes the lawyer's review. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each need to the AI solution pattern that usually fits it best.

options.text: Rule-based automation
Fine-tuning
AI agent
Predictive machine learning
Retrieval-augmented generation

slots.text: Answer questions from current internal documents, with sources
Predict which customers are likely to leave
Carry out a multi-step task across several systems
Keep a consistent specialised style across many outputs

questions.explanation: Retrieval grounds answers in current content, predictive models score likely outcomes from history, agents plan and act across systems, and fine-tuning adapts a model's behaviour or style. Rule-based automation fits fixed logic, which none of these needs describes. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question best helps a team choose the most practical AI solution pattern?

options.text: What is the simplest pattern that meets the need with acceptable risk?
Which pattern lets the team avoid changing its current process?
Which pattern uses the very newest and most capable model on the market?
Which pattern would impress the board most at the next review?

questions.explanation: Practical choice starts from the need and works up from the simplest option: a prompt, then retrieval, then fine-tuning or agents only when the simpler ones fall short. Novelty and avoiding process change lead to over-built or bolted-on solutions. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company adds an AI summary button to its existing claims screen, but adjusters still re-key data and wait days for approvals. Which description fits?

options.text: A Frontier use case that needs a time-boxed experiment
AI embedded in the old process, with little change to the flow
An AI-Native redesign of the whole claims process from end to end
A multi-agent system that coordinates the adjusters

questions.explanation: Adding AI to one step of an unchanged process gives a local gain while the delays elsewhere remain. An AI-Native approach would rethink the whole flow, for example extracting data automatically and routing simple claims straight through. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When does fine-tuning become a sensible pattern instead of prompting or RAG?

options.text: When the knowledge the model needs changes every week
When simpler options cannot reach the behaviour needed
When the answers must cite the documents they come from
When the team wants to start quickly with little data

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning needs good training data, effort and re-running as needs change, so it is usually chosen after prompting and retrieval fall short, for example for a specialised format or style at high volume. Changing knowledge and cited sources point to RAG instead. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An HR team wants to automate new-hire set-up: create accounts, order a laptop and book induction sessions in three separate systems. Which pattern fits?

options.text: A RAG assistant over the onboarding policy pages and checklists
An agent with scoped tools and checks at the risky steps
A model fine-tuned on past onboarding tickets
A predictive model that scores each new hire

questions.explanation: Action across several systems needs an agent that can call tools, with permissions limited to the task and checks where mistakes are costly. Retrieval and fine-tuning improve answers, not the ability to act. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An engineer reports '92 percent precision and 60 percent recall' for a fraud model. Which business translation is accurate?

options.text: It is right 92 percent of the time on every transaction
Most flagged cases are real fraud, but it misses many fraud cases
It catches most fraud, but many of the cases it flags are false alarms
It finds 60 percent more fraud than the old rules did

questions.explanation: Precision is the share of flagged cases that are truly fraud; recall is the share of all fraud that gets flagged. High precision with low recall means few false alarms but much missed fraud, which the business must weigh against the cost of each. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How should a product manager explain hallucination risk to a sales director?

options.text: It can state wrong facts confidently, so key claims need checking
It means the AI copies text from other companies' websites
It is a rare bug that the vendor will fix in its next model release
It occasionally crashes, so keep a backup of each document

questions.explanation: In business terms, the risk is plausible but false content that looks as reliable as true content, so outputs that matter are checked against sources. It is a property of how the models work, not a rare bug awaiting a fix. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A sponsor asks whether to switch to a cheaper, smaller model. Which answer frames the trade-off in business terms?

options.text: It depends on the model's architecture and how it was trained
Lower cost per request; test if its quality is enough here
Smaller models have fewer parameters, so benchmark scores drop
Use the largest model available, just to be on the safe side

questions.explanation: Business language turns a technical choice into cost, quality and risk for the task at hand, with a way to decide, here a quality test. Parameter counts and architecture are true but do not help a sponsor decide. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement translates 'the model has a 128,000-token context window' for a business audience?

options.text: It can store 128,000 customer records for later use
It has been trained on 128,000 company documents
It can answer 128,000 questions before it needs a reset
It can read a few hundred pages of text in one request

questions.explanation: A context window is how much text the model can consider in one go, and 128,000 tokens is roughly a few hundred pages. It is not storage, training data or a usage limit. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An IT lead says: 'RAG adds two seconds of retrieval latency per query.' How would you put this to a customer service manager?

options.text: Answers take about two seconds longer but draw on our documents
The system goes offline for two seconds after each question
Retrieval doubles the cost of running the service for each customer
Agents must wait two seconds before typing each new question

questions.explanation: Good translation states the effect on the user and the benefit bought with it, so the manager can judge whether two seconds matters for their customers. The distractors misstate what latency means. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest business framing of a pilot result?

options.text: Draft replies cut handling time by 30%, with no rise in complaints
Token usage averaged 1,800 per conversation during the pilot
The model reached a BLEU score of 0.42 on our customer support test set
The team fine-tuned three checkpoints and chose the second one

questions.explanation: Business stakeholders decide on outcomes such as time, cost, quality and risk, so a result framed that way, including a guard measure such as complaints, supports a decision. Technical metrics belong in the appendix. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A COO wants 'AI to reduce delivery delays'. What is the most useful first step toward a realistic solution?

options.text: Choose the most advanced model on the market for the whole job
Ask each depot to start using a chatbot of its own choice
Set a target of zero delays within the next three months
Find where delays arise and which data describes those steps

questions.explanation: A realistic solution starts from the specific problem and the data available: where delays happen, why, and what is recorded about them. Picking a model or a target first skips the analysis that decides whether AI can help. Topic 4.5, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team proposes a model to predict machine failures, but sensor data exists for only two months and is full of gaps. What should the plan include first?

options.text: Dropping the idea, since data gaps make AI impossible here
Training the model now and correcting its errors once it is live
Work to collect and clean enough data before building the model
Using a larger model so that it makes up for the missing data

questions.explanation: Models learn from data, so a data plan covering collection, quality and history often comes before the model; meanwhile simpler rules or monitoring may help. A bigger model cannot invent the failure patterns that the data lacks. Topic 4.5, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which element belongs in a practical AI implementation plan?

options.text: A list of each AI tool that the company might one day want to buy
A promise that AI will replace the team within a year
A baseline, a success measure and a date to decide on scaling
A rule that the plan is not reviewed until it is done

questions.explanation: A practical plan defines where things stand now, what improvement counts as success and when the evidence will be reviewed, so the team can scale, adjust or stop. Open-ended promises and tool lists give nothing to decide against. Topic 4.5, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A bank wants a chatbot to answer questions about customers' own accounts. Which data requirement matters most in the design?

options.text: A copy of every customer's history in the chatbot prompt
A list of questions that rival chatbots can answer
Secure, current access to each customer's own data alone
A large archive of public financial news to train on

questions.explanation: Account questions need current data for the signed-in customer only, through authenticated access with strict permissions. Loading many customers' data into prompts would be a serious privacy failure. Topic 4.5, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A manager asks for a fully automated AI system to approve expense claims. Which realistic alternative should be proposed first?

options.text: Staff approve claims by hand while AI writes all the monthly reports
AI rejects any claim above the average amount automatically
AI checks claims against policy and flags exceptions for a person
AI approves each claim, and auditors review a sample each year

questions.explanation: Starting with AI as a checker that handles the routine and routes exceptions to people delivers value quickly while evidence about accuracy builds, and autonomy can grow later. Full automation from day one carries the most risk with the least evidence. Topic 4.5, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI solution is meant to speed up answers to supplier queries. Which success measure fits best?

options.text: Number of AI features shipped in the first quarter
Time from query to correct answer, with accuracy checked
Number of employees who have opened the AI tool
Number of tokens the AI tool processes each day

questions.explanation: Measures should reflect the business outcome the solution was built for, here speed of resolution, with a quality check so that speed is not bought with wrong answers. Logins, tokens and features count activity, not value. Topic 4.5, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI vendor's demo looks impressive. What is the best next step before signing?

options.text: Ask the vendor for more demos with new examples
Choose the vendor whose model is largest
Sign quickly before the vendor's discount expires
Run a short pilot on the company's own data and tasks

questions.explanation: Demos are tuned to look good, so a time-boxed pilot on real tasks and data, with agreed measures, shows how the product performs in context. Discount deadlines and model size are not evidence of fit. Topic 4.6, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI vendor plans to retire the model version that a company's product relies on. Which contract term protects the company most?

options.text: A fixed price per user for each of the next five years
A logo placement on the vendor's own website and slides
A right to inspect the vendor's data centres once a year
Notice of changes well ahead, with time to test and move

questions.explanation: Models are updated and retired often, and a new version can change outputs, so contracts should give notice of changes and a migration window, ideally with version pinning. Price and site visits matter less to day-to-day reliability. Topic 4.6, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation criterion best separates two AI vendors whose demos look equally good?

options.text: The number of customer logos that each vendor shows on its website
The size of each vendor's team at the industry event
How recently each vendor announced a new model version
Measured results on a test set built from the company's real tasks

questions.explanation: A shared, realistic test set turns impressions into comparable evidence of quality, cost and failure modes. Customer logos and announcement dates say little about fit for this company's work. Topic 4.6, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Six months after selecting an AI vendor, a company sees answer quality falling. What should vendor management do?

options.text: Stop measuring quality to avoid a dispute with the vendor
Wait for the annual renewal to mention it to the vendor
Switch vendors at once without looking into the cause
Raise it against the agreed quality measures and review the fix

questions.explanation: Managing a vendor means tracking performance against agreed measures and acting when it slips, which may reveal a model change, a data issue or misuse. Waiting a year or switching without diagnosis both waste the evidence. Topic 4.6, lesson “4.3-4.6 · Solution patterns, business language, realistic plans and vendors”. Not checked against a public page.

notes.front: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
notes.back: Grounding a model's answer in content retrieved at question time.
notes.explanation: RAG lets a model use private or current data without changing its weights.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes

notes.front: What is composite AI?
notes.back: Combining machine learning, rules-based systems and LLMs in one solution.
notes.explanation: Each technique does the part it is best at.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: What separates an AI agent from a plain LLM chat?
notes.back: An agent decides on steps and calls tools to act toward a goal.
notes.explanation: A chat returns text; an agent can act, which is why it needs more governance.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption

notes.text: Core parts of an agent: a {{c1::model}} to reason, {{c2::instructions}} to bound it, {{c3::tools}} to act and {{c4::memory}} to keep state.
notes.explanation: Retrieval of grounding knowledge is often listed as a fifth part.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption

notes.front: Hallucination
notes.back: A fluent, confident output that is false or unsupported.
notes.explanation: Grounding and human checking reduce the risk; neither removes it.

notes.front: Copilot
notes.back: An AI assistant that works beside a user and offers suggestions to accept or edit.
notes.explanation: Contrast with an autonomous agent, which completes work independently.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · AI agents in Azure Cosmos DB (copilots and autonomous agents)

notes.front: Fine-tuning or RAG: which one changes the model's weights?
notes.back: Fine-tuning. RAG only changes what is in the prompt.
notes.explanation: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour and style; RAG supplies facts.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Retrieval augmented generation and indexes

notes.front: Generative AI
notes.back: AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video or code, from patterns learned in data.
notes.explanation: Predictive ML scores or labels; generative AI produces something new.

notes.front: What does an LLM do at its core?
notes.back: Predicts the next token, over and over, from patterns in huge amounts of text.
notes.explanation: It produces likely text, not checked facts.

notes.front: Why does an LLM give out-of-date facts?
notes.back: Its knowledge stops at its training cut-off unless current data is put in the prompt.
notes.explanation: Lowering temperature does not help; retrieval or pasted data does.

notes.front: Foundation model
notes.back: A large model trained on broad data, then adapted to many tasks by prompting, retrieval or fine-tuning.
notes.explanation: LLMs are the best-known example.

notes.text: {{c1::Deep learning}} is part of {{c2::machine learning}}, which is part of {{c3::artificial intelligence}}.
notes.explanation: The reversed nesting is a common distractor.

notes.front: Supervised learning
notes.back: Learning from examples that carry the right answer, such as emails labelled spam or not spam.
notes.explanation: Used for classification and prediction.

notes.front: Unsupervised learning
notes.back: Finding structure, such as clusters, in data that has no labels.
notes.explanation: Customer segments found without predefined groups.

notes.front: Parameters (weights)
notes.back: The internal values a model learns in training, which shape its outputs.
notes.explanation: Not the settings chosen per request, such as temperature.

notes.front: Natural language processing (NLP)
notes.back: The field of AI that works with human language in text or speech.
notes.explanation: LLMs are its leading technology; it is not a programming language.

notes.front: Token
notes.back: A piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads or writes; usage and limits are counted in these units.
notes.explanation: Roughly four characters of English per token.

notes.front: Context window
notes.back: The most text, in tokens, that a model can consider at once.
notes.explanation: Input beyond it is cut off or poorly used; retrieval sends only what is relevant.

notes.front: Temperature
notes.back: A setting for how random the choice of next token is: higher means more varied output.
notes.explanation: More varied, not more correct.

notes.front: Embedding
notes.back: A list of numbers representing the meaning of content, so similar meanings sit close together.
notes.explanation: RAG uses embeddings to find relevant passages.

notes.front: Grounded output
notes.back: Output based on supplied sources, such as retrieved documents, rather than the model's general training.
notes.explanation: The opposite of hallucination.

notes.front: What separates Semi-Automatic Agents from Full-Autonomous Agents?
notes.back: The approval step: at level 4 a person approves before the agent acts; at level 5 it acts alone.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

notes.text: RAG ingestion: {{c1::collect}} documents, {{c2::chunk}} them, {{c3::embed}} each chunk, {{c4::index}} the chunks and embeddings.
notes.explanation: Only then can questions be matched against the content.

notes.front: A RAG assistant is confidently wrong. Where do you look first?
notes.back: At the content and retrieval: stale documents, poor chunking, missing permissions or the wrong passages.
notes.explanation: Not at fine-tuning, temperature or context size.

notes.text: In composite AI, {{c1::rules}} enforce exact limits, {{c2::machine learning}} predicts from data and {{c3::LLMs}} handle language.
notes.explanation: Each technique does the part it is best at.

notes.front: Is one very large model composite AI?
notes.back: No. Composite AI combines different techniques, each with a clear job.
notes.explanation: Look for two or more techniques in the design.

notes.text: An agent loops: {{c1::plan}}, {{c2::act}} through a tool, {{c3::observe}} the result, then adjust.
notes.explanation: A tool result can change the next step.

notes.front: Tool use (agents)
notes.back: Calling functions or APIs to fetch data or take an action in another system.
notes.explanation: Tools define what an agent can do, and what it can damage.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · AI agent adoption

notes.front: An agent keeps calling the same tool without finishing. What fixes it?
notes.back: A cap on steps or tool calls, with a hand-off to a person.
notes.explanation: More context or a higher temperature does not stop a loop.

notes.front: What can a plain LLM with no tools do in other systems?
notes.back: Nothing: it turns a prompt into text. Acting needs tools and an agent loop.
notes.explanation: A read-only tool also cannot change anything.

notes.front: When is a single LLM call better than an agent?
notes.back: When the task is one step on supplied input with a person reviewing.
notes.explanation: Simpler designs are cheaper, easier to test and safer.

notes.front: Agentic AI approach
notes.back: Giving AI a goal and letting it plan, act, check and adapt within limits that people set.
notes.explanation: From asking for an answer to assigning an outcome.

notes.front: Multi-agent system
notes.back: Specialised agents that pass work to each other toward one goal, often under an orchestrator.
notes.explanation: Copies of one agent for scale are just deployment.

notes.front: Orchestrator
notes.back: The agent that coordinates others: it splits the work, routes tasks and combines results.
notes.explanation: Not a retriever and not a guardrail.

notes.front: Guardrail
notes.back: A control that constrains what an agent can do or say, such as a limit, an allow-list or an approval gate.
notes.explanation: A request in the prompt is not a guardrail.

notes.front: Observability (agents)
notes.back: Logs and traces of each step, tool call and reason, so autonomous work can be audited and explained.
notes.explanation: Without it, even a correct action cannot be explained.

notes.text: A custom GPT is configured with {{c1::instructions}}, {{c2::knowledge files}} and optional {{c3::actions}}.
notes.explanation: No weights change: it is configured, not trained.

notes.front: What lets a custom GPT update a CRM?
notes.back: An action that connects it to the CRM's API.
notes.explanation: Knowledge files only give it material to read.

notes.front: Why keep confidential files out of a shared custom GPT?
notes.back: Users can often draw out the content of its knowledge files by asking.
notes.explanation: Instructions are guidance, not guarantees.

notes.text: The study guide names three principles of responsible AI: {{c1::fairness}}, {{c2::transparency}} and {{c3::accountability}}.
notes.explanation: Fair outcomes, openness about AI use and its limits, and people who stay answerable.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: What does accountability mean for an AI system?
notes.back: Named people remain answerable for the system and its outcomes.
notes.explanation: 'The model decided' is not an owner.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Responsible AI for agent design

notes.front: Which GDPR principle limits collection to what is needed for the purpose?
notes.back: Data minimisation.
notes.explanation: Purpose limitation is about reuse; storage limitation is about how long data is kept.

sources.title: GDPR Article 5 · Principles

notes.front: Is pseudonymised data still personal data under the GDPR?
notes.back: Yes, while it can be linked back to a person with additional information.
notes.explanation: Only anonymous information is outside the regulation.

sources.title: GDPR Recital 26 · Anonymous and pseudonymised data

notes.front: What does GDPR Article 22 give a person?
notes.back: The right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
notes.explanation: Typical example: an automated loan refusal with no human involved.

sources.title: GDPR Article 22 · Automated individual decision-making

notes.front: Whom does the CCPA protect?
notes.back: Residents of California.
notes.explanation: It includes rights to know, delete, correct and opt out of sale or sharing. Not verified against the official page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Indirect prompt injection
notes.back: Malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page or file.
notes.explanation: In direct injection the attacker types the instruction into the prompt.

sources.title: OWASP GenAI · LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection

notes.front: Which control limits the damage an agent can do if it is manipulated?
notes.back: Least privilege: each tool has only the permissions the task needs.
notes.explanation: Add human approval for high-impact actions.

sources.title: OWASP GenAI · LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency

notes.text: The NIST AI RMF core functions are {{c1::govern}}, {{c2::map}}, {{c3::measure}} and {{c4::manage}}.
notes.explanation: Govern is cross-cutting and runs through the other three.

sources.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0 · Core functions

notes.front: Fairness (AI)
notes.back: Treating groups of people equitably, shown by comparing outcomes and error rates across groups.
notes.explanation: Removing a protected attribute is not enough, because proxies remain.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Transparency (AI)
notes.back: People know they are dealing with AI, what it is for and what it can and cannot do.
notes.explanation: A chatbot posing as a human adviser fails it.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Explainability
notes.back: Being able to give the reasons behind a particular output, such as the main factors in a decision.
notes.explanation: Publishing code is transparency, not an explanation of one decision.

notes.front: Model card
notes.back: A document of a model's intended use, data, limits and test results.
notes.explanation: Supports transparency and helps users judge fit.

notes.front: Inclusiveness
notes.back: A system works for the full range of people who use it, such as different accents, abilities or languages.
notes.explanation: Fix with representative data and testing with those users.

notes.front: What is the core question of an AI impact assessment?
notes.back: Who could this system affect, and how could they be harmed?
notes.explanation: Cost and speed are not ethical questions.

notes.front: Which comes first in an ethical decision: can we, or should we?
notes.back: Should we. Feasibility and accuracy matter only once the use is acceptable.
notes.explanation: Legal is a minimum, not proof of ethics.

notes.text: Three ways to test a decision: {{c1::consequences}} (best outcomes), {{c2::duties}} (rules and rights), {{c3::virtue}} (good character).
notes.explanation: Frameworks often use all three.

notes.front: NIST AI RMF: which function lists uses, users and risks, and which tests for bias?
notes.back: Map identifies context and risks; Measure assesses and tracks them.
notes.explanation: Govern sets policy; Manage acts on the risks.

sources.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0 · Core functions

notes.front: Direct prompt injection
notes.back: A user types instructions into the input to override the system's rules.
notes.explanation: Indirect injection hides them in content the model reads.

sources.title: OWASP GenAI · LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection

notes.front: Jailbreak
notes.back: A prompt crafted to get a model past its safety rules, often through role-play or framing.
notes.explanation: Safety cannot rest on the model's instructions alone.

sources.title: OWASP GenAI · LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection

notes.front: Data poisoning
notes.back: Planting bad data in what a model learns from or retrieves, so it misbehaves.
notes.explanation: Control and review data sources.

notes.front: Red teaming
notes.back: Adversarial testing: deliberately attacking a system to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
notes.explanation: Not load testing, which checks volume.

notes.front: A video call from the 'CFO' urgently asks for a transfer. What do you do?
notes.back: Verify through a separate, known channel before acting.
notes.explanation: Faces and voices can be cloned.

notes.front: Which GDPR principle bars reuse of personal data for an incompatible aim?
notes.back: Purpose limitation.
notes.explanation: Data minimisation limits how much is collected.

sources.title: GDPR Article 5 · Principles

notes.front: When is data anonymous under the GDPR?
notes.back: When people cannot be identified by means reasonably likely to be used.
notes.explanation: Birth date plus postcode can still single people out.

sources.title: GDPR Recital 26 · Anonymous and pseudonymised data

notes.text: CCPA rights include the right to {{c1::know}}, to {{c2::delete}}, to {{c3::correct}} and to {{c4::opt out}} of sale or sharing.
notes.explanation: Erasure and restriction are GDPR terms.

notes.front: Does the GDPR apply to a company with no office in the EU?
notes.back: Yes, if it offers goods or services to people in the EU or monitors their behaviour.
notes.explanation: Article 3, territorial scope.

sources.title: GDPR Article 3 · Territorial scope

notes.front: Few-shot prompting
notes.back: Putting a few example inputs and outputs in the prompt to show the behaviour wanted.
notes.explanation: The examples condition one request; nothing is retrained.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Prompt engineering techniques

notes.front: How do you stop a model inventing an answer that is not in the text?
notes.back: Give it an out: tell it to reply 'not found' when the answer is absent.
notes.explanation: Stressing accuracy alone leaves it no permitted alternative.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Prompt engineering techniques

notes.front: What should a RAG prompt tell the model to do?
notes.back: Answer from the provided context, cite sources, and say when the context lacks the answer.
notes.explanation: Otherwise it falls back on general training.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · RAG prompt engineering

notes.front: What does a strong image prompt describe?
notes.back: Subject, setting, framing, lighting and style.
notes.explanation: Praise words such as 'beautiful' give the generator nothing to draw.

notes.front: What does a video prompt need that a still-image prompt does not?
notes.back: Camera movement and the order in which the action unfolds.
notes.explanation: Video adds time, so describe the sequence.

notes.front: Where does human review belong in an AI-assisted workflow?
notes.back: Before the irreversible step, on the cases the AI flags or is unsure about.
notes.explanation: Review after the fact cannot change the outcome.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Which prompt pattern surfaces hidden project risks?
notes.back: Share the plan and assumptions, ask the model to imagine failure and list the causes.
notes.explanation: Then check each risk against what the team knows.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: How can AI help with difficult feedback?
notes.back: By reframing it as open questions about what was expected and what was missed.
notes.explanation: Remove names and identifying details first.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: What makes a good micro-plan?
notes.back: A small, specific, time-bound action with a visible result.
notes.explanation: Example: draft two status reports with AI this week and note the time saved.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.text: An effective prompt states the {{c1::task}}, {{c2::context}}, {{c3::audience}}, {{c4::constraints}} and {{c5::format}}.
notes.explanation: Add examples and a fallback where needed.

notes.front: Why mark off pasted material in a prompt?
notes.back: So the model can tell what to do from what to work on.
notes.explanation: Also put key instructions first and restate them at the end.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Prompt engineering techniques

notes.front: One prompt asks for research, a pricing model and an email, and all come back shallow. Fix?
notes.back: Split it into steps and review each before the next.
notes.explanation: Breaking the task down is a standard technique.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · Prompt engineering techniques

notes.front: The first answer is close but too long and formal. Next step?
notes.back: Give targeted feedback and ask for a revision.
notes.explanation: More efficient than starting again.

notes.text: A RAG prompt says: answer from the {{c1::context}}, say what to do when it is {{c2::missing}}, {{c3::cite}} each claim, and treat passages as {{c4::data}}, not instructions.
notes.explanation: Also delimit and label passages with source and date.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn · RAG prompt engineering

notes.front: Two retrieved passages disagree. What should the prompt say?
notes.back: Prefer the newer or more authoritative source and mention the conflict.
notes.explanation: Never average or pick by position.

notes.front: The passages answer only part of a question. What should the answer do?
notes.back: Answer the supported part and say what the sources leave out.
notes.explanation: Silent gap-filling mixes grounded and ungrounded content.

notes.front: How do you keep a character consistent across generated images?
notes.back: Reuse one fixed description and, where possible, a reference image.
notes.explanation: Rewriting the description each time invites variation.

notes.front: Why is 'not a cartoon' a weak image prompt?
notes.back: It says what to avoid but not what to aim for; name the target style.
notes.explanation: State exclusions as well as the target.

notes.front: Name two responsible-use rules for generated images.
notes.back: Do not use a real person's likeness without consent; label generated images and do not fake real events.
notes.explanation: These are not prompt-craft issues.

notes.front: What comes first when redesigning a process with AI?
notes.back: Map the current steps and find where time and errors go.
notes.explanation: Then choose AI steps and human steps.

notes.front: Rubber-stamp review
notes.back: Reviewers approve AI output almost instantly, so the review no longer checks anything.
notes.explanation: Fix with risk-based routing and better evidence for reviewers.

notes.front: Automation bias
notes.back: The tendency to over-trust automated or AI output, especially under time pressure.
notes.explanation: Show sources and confidence, and audit a sample.

notes.front: What should a workflow do when the AI cannot decide?
notes.back: Hand the case to a named person with the context attached.
notes.explanation: Not a forced guess or an endless retry.

notes.front: What makes a question powerful for finding risks?
notes.back: It is open, specific and challenges an assumption.
notes.explanation: 'What would have to be true for this date to hold?'

notes.front: AI returned generic risks. Best follow-up?
notes.back: For each risk, ask for an early warning sign to watch for.
notes.explanation: Makes risks actionable.

notes.front: Why ask AI to play stakeholders when looking for risks?
notes.back: It surfaces risks from viewpoints the team does not hold.
notes.explanation: It prepares for, but does not replace, talking to them.

notes.front: What must AI keep when reframing an angry message into questions?
notes.back: Every concern; only the framing changes.
notes.explanation: Softening until nobody acts is a failure.

notes.front: Give a curious, not defensive, response to criticism.
notes.back: 'Tell me more about what happened and how it affected you.'
notes.explanation: Correcting or deflecting closes the conversation.

notes.front: AI gives five reframed questions. What do you do?
notes.back: Choose the two or three most relevant and adapt their wording.
notes.explanation: AI output is a draft, not a script.

notes.text: An AI opportunity summary: {{c1::challenge or goal}}, AI idea, {{c2::measurable outcome}}, main {{c3::assumption}}, and a small {{c4::first step}}.
notes.explanation: A few sentences, not a project plan.

notes.front: How should an AI opportunity summary open?
notes.back: With a concrete, measured problem, such as 'agents spend 40% of their time searching'.
notes.explanation: Not with hype or the technology.

notes.front: A summary 'describes a tool, not an opportunity'. What is missing?
notes.back: The challenge or goal the tool would address.
notes.explanation: Features are not value.

notes.front: What kind of first step suits an opportunity summary?
notes.back: A small, time-boxed trial measured against a baseline.
notes.explanation: Not a company-wide rollout.

notes.text: A micro-plan names one {{c1::task}}, a {{c2::trigger}} or time, a {{c3::measure}} and a {{c4::review}} date.
notes.explanation: Small, specific and time-bound.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: What makes a new AI habit more likely to stick?
notes.back: Tying it to an existing routine or trigger.
notes.explanation: 'When there is time' rarely happens.

notes.front: A micro-plan is not saving time. What now?
notes.back: Adjust the prompt or choose a better-suited task, then try again.
notes.explanation: It is an experiment, not a verdict on AI.

notes.text: EDGE stands for {{c1::Exponential}}, {{c2::Disruptive}}, {{c3::Generative}} and {{c4::Emergent}}.
notes.explanation: The four forces the course uses to make the AI-Native case in business terms.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.text: AI use cases are classified as {{c1::Stable}}, {{c2::Evolving}} or {{c3::Frontier}}.
notes.explanation: By maturity and future potential. The definitions come from the course.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: How do Scaled Agile's public articles describe an AI-Native organization?
notes.back: One designed with AI at the forefront, as a cultural foundation.
notes.explanation: Contrast: embedded AI adds AI components to existing systems.

sources.title: Scaled Agile blog · AI-Native articles

notes.front: Name the three reasons AI initiatives fail, per Scaled Agile's public articles.
notes.back: No clear strategic vision, a workforce not upskilled, experiments not scaled.
notes.explanation: All three are organisational, not technical.

sources.title: Scaled Agile blog · AI certifications for product managers

notes.front: How do you put an AI trade-off into business language?
notes.back: State its effect on speed, cost, quality and risk.
notes.explanation: Leave parameters and architecture out.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Which vendor question matters most for protecting data?
notes.back: Is our data used to train their models, and where is it kept?
notes.explanation: Also ask about export rights to limit lock-in.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Exponential growth (EDGE)
notes.back: Capability compounds and cost per task falls fast, so plans go stale within months.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Disruptive (EDGE)
notes.back: New entrants use AI to overturn established players and business models.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Generative (EDGE)
notes.back: AI creates content, code and designs at very low cost, which changes how work is done.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Emergent (EDGE)
notes.back: Abilities appear that nobody designed, so value and risk are found by experimenting.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Stable use case
notes.back: Proven patterns, broad adoption and predictable results: adopt with standard controls.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Evolving use case
notes.back: Known patterns whose results still vary with data and design: pilot, measure, mature.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Frontier use case
notes.back: Little evidence in production and high uncertainty: small, time-boxed experiments.
notes.explanation: The study guide names this; the meaning given here is the author's reading. Check it against your workbook.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Exam study guide: AI-Native Foundations

notes.front: Which question picks the most practical AI solution pattern?
notes.back: What is the simplest pattern that meets the need with acceptable risk?
notes.explanation: Work up from a prompt, to retrieval, to fine-tuning or agents.

notes.front: When does fine-tuning make sense?
notes.back: When prompting and retrieval fall short of the needed behaviour, such as a specialised style at volume.
notes.explanation: Changing knowledge and cited sources point to RAG.

notes.front: AI added to one step of an unchanged process is called what, and what is the alternative?
notes.back: AI embedded in the old process; the alternative is an AI-Native redesign of the whole flow.
notes.explanation: Local gains, while delays elsewhere remain.

notes.text: {{c1::Precision}} is the share of flagged cases that are real; {{c2::recall}} is the share of real cases that get flagged.
notes.explanation: High precision, low recall: few false alarms, much missed.

notes.front: How do you translate an AI trade-off for a sponsor?
notes.back: State the effect on cost, time, quality and risk for this task, and how to decide.
notes.explanation: Technical metrics belong in the appendix.

notes.front: First step for 'AI to reduce delivery delays'?
notes.back: Find where delays arise and which data describes those steps.
notes.explanation: Not choosing a model first.

notes.text: A practical AI plan has a {{c1::baseline}}, a {{c2::success measure}} and a {{c3::decision date}} for scaling.
notes.explanation: So the team can scale, adjust or stop.

notes.front: Asked for full automation of expense approval, what do you propose first?
notes.back: AI checks claims against policy and flags exceptions for a person.
notes.explanation: Autonomy can grow with evidence.

notes.front: A vendor demo is impressive. Next step?
notes.back: A short pilot on the company's own data and tasks, with agreed measures.
notes.explanation: Demos are tuned to look good.

notes.text: Key AI vendor terms: whether your data {{c1::trains their models}}, the right to {{c2::export}} data and prompts, and {{c3::notice}} of model changes.
notes.explanation: Then manage against agreed measures.
